subject: Economics
title: Cost, Revenue, and Markets
outline: Concepts of cost: fixed, variable, total, average and marginal cost
Short-run and long-run cost curves and the envelope curve
Revenue concepts: total, average and marginal revenue
Profit maximisation rule MC = MR and the break-even point
Perfect competition: assumptions, equilibrium, shut-down point
Monopoly: sources, price and output determination, price discrimination, control
Monopolistic competition and oligopoly: features and behaviour
Comparison of market structures and efficiency

modules.title: Costs and Revenue of the Firm
modules.html:
1.1 Cost concepts

  • Fixed cost (FC) — does not vary with output: rent, insurance, salaries of permanent staff.
  • Variable cost (VC) — varies directly with output: raw materials, fuel, casual wages.
  • Total cost: \( TC = FC + VC \).
  • Average cost: \( AC = TC/Q = AFC + AVC \).
  • Marginal cost: \( MC = \dfrac{\Delta TC}{\Delta Q} \), the cost of producing one extra unit.

Other distinctions: explicit (money paid out) versus implicit (imputed cost of owner's own resources); opportunity cost; social cost = private cost + external cost.

1.2 Shape of the cost curves

AFC falls continuously because a fixed sum is spread over more units. AVC and AC are U-shaped because of increasing then diminishing returns. MC cuts both AVC and AC at their minimum points; when MC < AC, AC falls, and when MC > AC, AC rises. In the long run all factors are variable, so the long-run average cost curve is the envelope of short-run curves, falling with economies of scale and rising with diseconomies.

1.3 Revenue concepts

\( TR = P \times Q \); \( AR = TR/Q = P \); \( MR = \Delta TR/\Delta Q \). Under perfect competition price is constant so \( AR = MR \) and both are horizontal. Under imperfect competition the firm faces a downward-sloping AR curve and MR lies below AR.

1.4 Profit maximisation and break-even

$$ \pi = TR - TC, \qquad \text{maximised where } MC = MR \text{ and MC is rising} $$

The break-even point is where \( TR = TC \) (normal profit only):

$$ Q_{BE} = \frac{FC}{P - AVC} $$

A firm shuts down in the short run if price falls below AVC, and leaves the industry in the long run if price is below AC.

examples.q: A firm has FC = ₦120,000, AVC = ₦400 and sells at ₦700 per unit. Find the break-even output and the profit at 600 units.
Why does the marginal cost curve cut the average cost curve at its minimum?
examples.a: When MC is below AC it pulls the average down; when MC is above AC it pulls the average up. AC therefore stops falling and starts rising precisely where MC = AC, which is the minimum point of AC.

modules.title: Market Structures
modules.html:
2.1 Perfect competition

Assumptions: very many small buyers and sellers, homogeneous product, free entry and exit, perfect knowledge, perfect factor mobility, no transport cost, no government interference. The firm is a price taker with a horizontal demand curve.

Equilibrium: \( MC = MR = P = AR \). In the long run free entry drives profit to normal profit, where \( P = AC = MC \) at the minimum of AC — the most efficient outcome.

2.2 Monopoly

A single seller with no close substitute and barriers to entry. Sources: patents and copyright, control of raw material, legal franchise, huge capital requirement, natural monopoly (falling long-run costs), amalgamation.

The monopolist equates MC with MR, then charges the price on the demand (AR) curve above that output, so \( P > MC \) and supernormal profit can persist in the long run. Output is lower and price higher than under perfect competition.

Price discrimination — charging different prices in separate markets for the same product — requires market separation and different elasticities (e.g. student fares, export dumping, electricity tariffs). Monopoly is controlled by anti-trust legislation, price regulation, taxation, subsidised competition, nationalisation and removal of import barriers.

2.3 Monopolistic competition

Many sellers of differentiated products (branding, packaging, advertising), fairly free entry. The firm has a downward-sloping but elastic demand curve, earns supernormal profit in the short run and only normal profit in the long run, but produces with excess capacity because \( P > MC \) at equilibrium.

2.4 Oligopoly

A few large firms dominate; each is interdependent, so price changes provoke rival reactions. Features: price rigidity (kinked demand curve), heavy non-price competition, mutual interdependence, possible collusion in cartels (e.g. OPEC) or price leadership. Duopoly is a special case of two firms.

examples.q: A monopolist faces \( P = 100 - 2Q \) and \( TC = 20Q \). Find the profit-maximising output and price.
examples.a: TR = PQ = 100Q − 2Q², so MR = 100 − 4Q; MC = 20. Setting MR = MC: 100 − 4Q = 20 → Q = 20. Price = 100 − 2(20) = ₦60. Profit = TR − TC = (60 × 20) − (20 × 20) = ₦800.

examples.q: Why does a perfectly competitive firm earn only normal profit in the long run?
examples.a: Supernormal profit attracts new entrants because entry is free. Industry supply rises, market price falls, and entry continues until price equals average cost at its minimum, leaving only normal profit.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a fixed cost?
quiz.solution: Rent must be paid whether output is high, low or zero, so it does not vary with output.

options: Change in total cost from producing one more unit

quiz.q: Average fixed cost falls continuously as output rises because:
options: A constant fixed cost is spread over more units
quiz.solution: Dividing an unchanged fixed sum by a larger output gives a smaller figure each time.
Profit is greatest at the output where marginal cost equals marginal revenue with MC rising.

quiz.q: If FC = ₦60,000, price = ₦500 and AVC = ₦300, break-even output is:
Under perfect competition, the individual firm's demand curve is:
quiz.solution: The firm is a price taker: it can sell any quantity at the ruling market price, so AR = MR is horizontal.

quiz.q: In the long run a perfectly competitive firm earns:
quiz.solution: Free entry and exit eliminate abnormal profit, leaving normal profit where P = AC = MC.

quiz.q: A firm should shut down in the short run when price falls below:
quiz.solution: If price cannot cover AVC, producing adds to losses beyond the unavoidable fixed cost, so shutting down is better.

quiz.q: A monopolist's marginal revenue curve lies:
quiz.solution: Because price must be lowered to sell extra units, MR falls faster than AR and lies below it.

quiz.q: Which is a source of monopoly power?
quiz.solution: A patent gives the holder the exclusive legal right to produce, blocking competitors.

quiz.q: Price discrimination is possible only when:
options: Markets can be separated with different elasticities
quiz.solution: The seller must prevent resale between markets and face different demand elasticities to profit from charging different prices.

quiz.q: Product differentiation is the key feature of:
quiz.solution: Monopolistic competition has many firms selling similar but differentiated products through branding and packaging.

quiz.q: The kinked demand curve is used to explain price rigidity under:
quiz.solution: Under oligopoly rivals match price cuts but not price rises, producing a kink and hence stable prices.

quiz.q: An agreement among firms to fix output and price is a:
quiz.solution: A cartel is a formal collusive agreement, OPEC being the best-known example.

quiz.q: Excess capacity in monopolistic competition arises because at equilibrium:
quiz.solution: Output stops short of the minimum-cost level since price exceeds marginal cost, leaving unused capacity.
Social cost adds the external costs imposed on third parties, such as pollution, to the firm's private cost.

quiz.q: When MC is greater than AC, average cost is:
quiz.solution: A marginal value above the average pulls the average upward.
